utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May I, first of all, begin by taking the appearances.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. For the Prosecution, I'm Tom Hannis, assisted today by Jasmina Bosnjakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, and Eugene O'Sullivan appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: For Zupljanin Defence -- good morning, Your Honours. For Zupljanin Defence this morning, appearing Igor Pantelic and Dragan Krgovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. I -- I assume the persons who are even from other than an English speaking background are familiar with the concept of Murphy's law that anything that can go wrong will. In my office at home, I actually have a sign that Murphy was an optimist. And in that vain, Mr. Zecevic, despite the efforts that we thought we took yesterday to ensure that the procedural arrangements would be made to facilitate your communication with your client this morning, I understand there was a glitch. So the question is whether - notwithstanding what unfortunately went wrong - you are in a position to -- to -- you were in a position to take instructions on -- on the relevant issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. As a matter of fact, well, the glitches are happening as -- as we know, and you're correct, this is a Murphy's law. But, however, last night due to the transport which was due to start after -- at 7.00 or some minutes after, I had the opportunity to -- to talk to my client for half an hour, and this 15 minutes this morning, it was more than enough. So I'm ready and prepared to -- thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So the usher will escort the witness back to the stand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Something is buzzing in my ears.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We hear some buzzing sound or ... [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we've called for a technician to look into the issue, and someone will be here in a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, your sign in the office is -- is definitely true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I remind you, sir, that you're still on your oath.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Scekic.

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday in the course of examination-in-chief, you confirmed to my learned friend, Mr. Hannis, that the work on providing security for persons and facilities engaged one company in Pale, from a public security company, whose commander, I believe, came from Zvornik, Vukovic. I have to ask to you make a break for the -- between -- to make a pause between question and answer for the record. Let me summarise. You confirm there was a public security company in Pale, and their job was to provide security to physical persons and facilities, and Vukovic was their commander.

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. They secured VIP apartments and buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The name of that person is Vojo Vukovic. Does that jog your memory?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Vojo Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you talked about personal security to Minister Stanisic, and you mentioned in that respect Zoran Jasarevic as his driver?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Isn't it a fact that normally people who enjoy security details have drivers who are -- who double as body-guards?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if he didn't have a separate personal driver, then his driver would be his body-guard, and that job would be regulated and linked to the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the personal body-guard, in addition to this Zoran Jasarevic who was a driver, the personal guard to Mr. Stanisic was actually Goran Abazovic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that, because it was the public security sector who provided body-guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Yesterday, when you were talking about Dusko Malovic, on page 50 of the transcript, you said that you noted him as a striking, handsome man, whose father you knew, and then you were unable to recall his last name. And you said: "I know that shortly afterwards he was killed, but I can't remember the year. I think his last name was Malovic." And then you explained that you had been told he had been in the army, then he was demobilised, and he then worked as a body-guard to Minister Stanisic. You remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I accept all that, apart from one fact which may have been misinterpreted. I didn't know his father. But the colleagues who were in the VIP security section told me that he had been in the JNA, that he was demobilised, and he was now body-guard to Minister Stanisic. But I didn't know either the man or his father. Could have been misinterpreted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Probably. But I'm interested in this other thing. If I understood correctly what you said yesterday, that means that shortly after you noticed him and made inquiries about him, he was killed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was killed in Belgrade, and rumour had it later that he was killed by mistake. It was a case of mistaken identity. The real target was a man called Vukovic; not from Serbia, from Montenegro, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'll try to refresh your memory. Do you remember that Mr. Malovic was killed while riding in a war, together with Goran Vukovic, whose nickname was Majmun, Monkey, and was known in the criminal circles as the killer of another well-known criminal, Ljubo Zemunac. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I know that the target was Vukovic, somewhere from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Scekic, this assassination of Vukovic in which Dusko Malovic was killed as well, happened on the 12th of December, 1994, in Belgrade, outside the Yugoslav drama theatre. Does that refresh your memory?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know about the assassination, but I don't know the year.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, sir, from the time when, on the 15th of May, 1992, you took up your job in Pale, you stayed in Pale all the way until 1995, 1996?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I suppose then that you know that Mr. Stanisic was minister in two terms: First, in April until November 1992, when Djeric's government fell; and then for several months in the beginning of 1994. You know that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that. I know that Mr. Stanisic occupied that post twice and that there was a total of five ministers of internal affairs until the Dayton Accords. Some of them had a very shorter tenure, just a few months, and there were others who had absolutely nothing to do with the Ministry of Interior or the trade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Scekic, I put it to you that Dusko Malovic was on the security detail of Mr. Stanisic in Mr. Stanisic's second tenure as minister. That means in 1994, not in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him two or three times, together with the minister of the interior. Now in which period that was, I really don't know. I saw him a couple of times. I know he was a striking, handsome young man, and later we read in the newspaper there was this assassination in Belgrade and he was killed by mistake. Another man was supposed to be killed. And now I hear from you who that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, your position remains as it was yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Scekic, I'd like to start with the last question today. You told us that in 1992 where you were housed in doing your work. Did you remain in that location throughout the time until you retired, or did you move somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right at the beginning of 1992, I spent a while in hotel Bistrica which was the seat of the government, and then later, when Mr. Karadzic moved to the Famos building I made myself an office there, to be close to him, and it was also closer to all the VIPs who had security. There was the President there, the prime minister, and the government. The leadership of the State Security Service had moved to Bijeljina for a short while, because of a shortage of offices, and I stayed with a couple of other employees in the State Security Service in Kikinda; whereas, I had my office there Famos, in the building which housed the office of the President of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when did Mr. Karadzic move to Famos?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Did you understand the question, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you hear my question?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, let me ask again because your answer is not recorded. Do you know -- do you recall when Mr. Karadzic moved to Famos, approximately?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was sometime in early 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yesterday, when you were talking about having seen Mr. Malovic in the company of Mr. Stanisic, I believe you told us you saw that when Mr. Stanisic appeared to be going to visit Mr. Karadzic or Mr. Krajisnik, where they were located at that time, and I believe you had said that that location was at Panorama; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct, that's what I said. But it was 18 years ago. I allow the possibility that I also saw them outside Panorama. Now, whether only the Speaker of the Assembly remained there, or maybe he was visiting -- or maybe Karadzic was visiting Krajisnik, or they were in Famos, I don't know that anymore. But it's true that I saw Dusko Malovic two or three times with the minister. Now, whether Krajisnik was the one who was being visited or they were visiting Koljevic or Biljana Plavsic, because they were all -- they had their offices close by ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Wasn't part of the reason you recalled seeing Mr. Malovic with Mr. Stanisic at Panorama was because you were located just across the street at that time, in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the outset, for a short while, I was based in Hotel panorama, but later when the government moved to Bistrica hotel, I moved there with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In 1994, do you know where Mico Stanisic was when he was minister for the second time? Was he in Pale, was he Bijeljina, where was he primarily located?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mico Stanisic, in 1994, spent most of the time in Tron. It's a building -- I don't know how to explain. Some sort of catering establishment. It was called Tron. He may have spent a few nights on Jahorina as well, where the special unit was housed but most of the time he spent nights in Tron. That's where public security was based.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you tell the Judges where Tron was located? In what town or near what town?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Pale. I don't know how to explain more precisely. He was the closest -- the next close location was the government seat. Halfway between the government seat and the Assembly, let's say.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday, at page 69 -- oh.

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. And that's where the office of the minister of the interior was, in this Tron building.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how far was the Tron building located from Panorama?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe a kilometre, kilometre and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday, at page 69, line 14, Mr. Zecevic was discussing with you about the meeting in Pale that you went to, where Mr. Kijac and Mr. Stanisic were present and where it was discussed that there was going to be a new Serbian MUP created, and you were to return to your post and not follow directions of Muslim superiors, if those directions were contrary to the interest of Serbs. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said -- it was a short meeting. I said yesterday I allow the possibility that he may have been introduced as the future minister or already a minister. But the point of the entire meeting was that we were staying in our jobs, that a Muslim may be our chief but may not give us assignments that would be contrary to the interests of the Serb people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In trying to narrow down the date of that meeting, I'd like to ask you if you were aware of the issuance of a dispatch by Momo Mandic on the 31st of March where he invited all police officers of Serb nationality to put themselves at the disposition of the newly created Serbian MUP. Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. The dispatch could not have reached me directly. It could have reached the chief of the State Security Centre who would in turn forward it to the chiefs of departments. We were duty-bound, in respect of every dispatch that we may have received or any letter of appointment or any order, to place our initials on each and every dispatch to indicate that we were apprised of it. Since a Muslim, Munir Alibabic, was at the head of our service, I don't think that it ever crossed his mind to forward the dispatch for information to those of us who remained in the service and were of Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can we show the witness Exhibit P29.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Scekic, this is something you looked at yesterday. We looked at the photograph, but now I want to look at the news article that you started to read from yesterday. And my English translation of that caption is: April Fool Reality. I see we're still waiting for your B/C/S. If we could go to the bottom of the page in B/C/S. I don't know if you can read that hard copy underneath. The bold part is translated as: "Serbian members of the service already invited to join Serbian MUP." And then in the smaller print in the second line it says: "Momcilo Mandic, deputy minister, invited 'according to the constitution of the Serbian Republic, of Bosnia-Herzegovina' all police officers of Serbian nationality to put themselves at the disposition of 'MUP of Serbian Republic,' today on the 1st of April." You weren't aware of that? Here it's printed in Oslobodjenje on the 1st of April.

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Not from any of your colleagues, not from radio, not from TV?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have heard it. But then I heard many unpleasant things too about me as well. And to tell you the truth, I didn't really read the Oslobodjenje. I would read other Sarajevo papers. I would read Oslobodjenje only occasionally. There are certain illogical matters here. How can Delimustafic issue an appeal for unity --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. This wasn't a matter that was published in any of the other newspapers on or about the 1st of April, 1992, in Sarajevo? Is that what you're telling me?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fact that this was published in newspapers is not in dispute. I don't want it deny it. I may not have read it or I may have read it but since it was 18 years ago I forgot. I may well have read it and not remember it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The reason I'm asking is, if the Serbian MUP had been publically announced and all MUP employees of Serbian nationality invited to put themselves at the disposition of that newly created Serbian MUP on the 1st of April, would you not agree with me that the meeting you attended where you were told that a new Serbian MUP was going to be formed would have been -- that meeting would have been before the 1st of April?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said as much. It was held at the end of March or in early April. This is what I stated yesterday. I think it is more likely that it was held in the early days of April. I'm saying this because of the newspaper article published in Vecernje Novine which concerned me. At that point in time, I was already unable to go to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise to my friend. Your Honours, we are very tolerant this morning, it's Friday, maybe that's the reason. We are not objecting to the whole line of leading questions of my learned friend. So, please, Mr. Hannis, take care a little bit of the Rules. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At the meeting that you went to you told us that you were informed to return to your work and not follow directions of your Muslim supervisors. Let me ask you, if there was already a Serbian MUP in existence, why would you be told to go back to work for your Muslim supervisors? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm just -- just for the clarity, Mr. Hannis, it is not -- it is not the -- that they were -- they were not to follow the directions of their Muslim superiors. It is -- it is much more specified. You're misinterpreting the evidence of the witness, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you want to give me a page reference?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't find it but I believe everybody will remember that the witness said not to follow the directions of -- of Muslim superiors if they are not in interest of Serbia or contrary to the interests of Serbian people. That is the only reference I wanted to make. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Right. But my question is why would you go back to work with Muslim superiors when you're invited to join the Serbian MUP which did not have any Muslim superiors.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't -- I didn't -- I wasn't objecting to your question. I was just objecting to the -- to the previous line where -- where you -- where you didn't state fully the -- the evidence of this witness. That -- that was my objection, nothing else. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, let me ask the question again. If there was already a Serbian MUP formed at the time of your meeting, can you explain why you would have been directed to go back to work where there were Muslim superiors, instead of just going to work at the newly formed Serbian MUP?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I don't know that the Serbian MUP had been formed at the time. I suppose they would have informed us about it, and -- about the appointments. I suppose they would have informed us about the location of our offices in Pale, about the equipment we had at our disposal, and about the staff who were supposed to join us. This was a very brief meeting at which we were told that the Serbian MUP was being formed but that we would stay at our work because the secretary of the Sarajevo MUP remained the same, the same individual, even after that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think we're not in disagreement. You've told us that conditions that you were working under in late 1991 and 1992 were not very good, and why, if there were already a Serbian MUP in existence, would Serbian MUP employees, like yourself, be told to go back to that? That's why I think the meeting you attended must have been before April 1st. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do understand. But then I did say that it was in late March or early April. When I cast my mind back to that period, I do believe it's more likely that it was in early April, because the lies were published about me in Vecernje Novine on the 7th and by that time, I was already unable to go to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I -- I understand. And I understand that that was probably more on your mind than anything else, the newspaper article that was being published about you personally. Is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The last thing I want to ask you about. Yesterday, at page 76, line 10 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, forgive me for not being fully aware of the status of this article, is that in evidence or do you wish to tender it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It is in evidence, Your Honours, as P29.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yesterday, at page 76 line 2, Mr. Zecevic was talking to you about how it was in the former Socialist Republic of Bosnia, where the under-secretary for state security actually was paid more than the minister, or the secretary. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not that pay discrepancy continued to exist in the Republika Srpska? Did Mr. Skipina or Mr. Kijac get paid more than Minister Stanisic. Do you know?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. Pay was not something that was discussed. I had my pay as a chief of administration and that was ranked third, I think, in the hierarchy, because then you had the state Presidency, they were the top echelon, then the ministers, and then us as chiefs of departments. We always had a 10 percent higher wage than those who were in the rest of the ministry. And I could buy ten cartons of cigarettes with my pay at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Related to that, you were then asked whether or not you agreed that in the former Bosnia-Herzegovina, before the war in 1992, whether the position of the under-secretary for state security was actually a bit stronger, even than the position of secretary, or minister for internal affairs, and I think you -- you agreed with that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For us in the State Security Service, the under-secretary was to us what a general is to a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand. And I think part of the -- part of your reasoning based on your answer was you said sometimes before the war he, meaning the under-secretary, had to keep informed the President of the Central Committee or the President of the Presidency and possibly the prime minister. My question is: In the Republika Srpska, do you know what the situation was? Would you say Mr. Skipina or Mr. Kijac were stronger as under-secretaries for state security than the minister himself?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Skipina's tenure was very short before the war. Mr. Kijac was only an operative, and I think that he deserved to become the under-secretary of the State Security Service. The under-secretary informed the -- and briefed the minister of the interior; that was his duty. Equally so, he could turn to the President of the Republic, or the prime minister, wherever he felt that there was urgent information to be conveyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In your answer yesterday at page 77, you said -- it depended on who the minister was. You said: "Sometimes the under-secretary would go through the minister to inform the president or the prime minister, et cetera. Do you know what the relationship was in the RS MUP between Skipina and later Kijac in terms of whether or not they directly informed Karadzic and Djeric, those others, directly or through Minister Stanisic. Do you know?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you anything about it. I know that Skipina was there only for a short time and that Kijac subsequently become the under-secretary. The minister's seat was not in Pale either, so he could not be reached directly. It depended on the ministry. Some of the ministers were seated in Banja Luka; others in Bijeljina. When the State Security Service moved to Bijeljina, most likely the minister's seat was in Bijeljina. The minister was Zivko Rakic from the Bosnian Krajina and he was there rarely. He was a minister who hailed from Ilijas. He was a physics teacher. His tenure was also very short. No sooner did he assume his position than he was replaced. I wouldn't be able to tell you exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And I apologies. There was one last topic I needed to go back to. Yesterday at page 65, beginning at line 18, you and Mr. Zecevic were talking about Munir Alibabic, who you described as a great professional, and you both mentioned the fact that Mr. Alibabic had, back in the early 1980s, investigated Mr. Izetbegovic, and as a result of that investigation Mr. Izetbegovic was tried and sent to prison for a while. Isn't it a fact that within your service, the State Security Service, which later became the National Security Service, state security people were investigating the leaders of the nationalist parties in 1990 and 1991, Karadzic, Krajisnik, Izetbegovic, whoever the Croatians were. All of those leaders were being investigated by state security; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Munir Alibabic was leading the investigation into Alija Izetbegovic. Not only was he a member of the team, he was at the head of it. As for Karadzic and Krajisnik, I don't know about that. It was not in my line of duty. I do know that they had been convicted by the public security branch for white-collar crime. It involved the construction of weekend cottages in Pale or somewhere. I know that they were the subject of examination of the Public Security Service, and that was not part of my work.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what would you say about when in 1991 these nationalist politicians came into power and were making appointments into the MUP, how would you describe their attitude toward the State Security Service?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody would give up on the MUP, because that gave you the leverage and power. Every country's strength is measured by the strength of their police force. Unfortunately, the Serbian Democratic Party did not have either the power or will to get any vital positions. It got peripheral positions. It should have at least tried to get the security services centre, but they didn't even get that. They only got the city of Sarajevo structure which meant little. As for the sporadic positions that they got in the Ministry of the Interior, they were insignificant, compared to 120 posts that were envisaged only for the security services centre in Sarajevo. The problem is that the --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. I'm asking about the attitude of all nationalist politicians --

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- security services did not resolve its systematic problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- toward the State Security Service in general. They didn't trust the state security, did they?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't put it that way. Alija Izetbegovic nominated Munir Alibabic. He had always -- he had even wanted him to become the minister of the interior; whereas, it was precisely Munir Alibabic who had sent him to prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Didn't the public security side have some reserve or distrust for the state security side? Just because of the nature of the work you did on your side.

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, there was a degree of that. Because they wore uniforms, we -- we called them dust biters, just as would you -- as the airmen would call the infantrymen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you know what they called you guys on the state security side?

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that, and I would dearly like to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I -- I don't know. I know in other jurisdictions sometimes the state police, security police, CIA, are referred to as spooks. Because no one knows what they're doing or where they're going.

utterances.speaker: MILAN SCEKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is possible. In Montenegro, they referred to them as spies.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, for attending and assisting the Tribunal. You are now released as a witness, and we wish you a safe journey back to your home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. So the usher will now escort you from the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, that is it until Monday afternoon, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. So we take the adjournment to Monday, at 2.15, and I wish everyone a safe weekend. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
